newsitem.title: USA: Weather outlook bleak for U.S. shuttle launch.
newsitem.headline: Weather outlook bleak for U.S. shuttle launch.

text.p: Forecasts of bad weather are dimming hopes that the Columbia space shuttle can take off as scheduled, NASA officials said on Wednesday.
The $2 billion spaceship is due to blast off from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 2:50 p.m. (1950 GMT) on Friday on a 16-day science mission.
But Columbia's chances of lifting off on time were just 1-in-10 because of a forecast for high winds and cloudy skies, shuttle weather officer Ed Priselac said.

In addition, rough seas and gusty conditions offshore could damage the shuttle's reusable rocket boosters when they splash down in the Atlantic, he said. Recovery of the spent rockets would also be difficult in the heaving seas.
"I really don't see a lot of options until we get well into next week," Priselac said. "Unfortunately, things don't look very good."

NASA officials were also waiting for an Atlas rocket to blast off from Cape Canaveral on Wednesday afternoon. If the weather delays that launch until Thursday, Columbia's launch will be pushed back to Saturday so U.S. Air Force tracking equipment can be reprogrammed.
The shuttle's countdown was proceeding smoothly after the resolution of a last-minute technical problem with one of the craft's three electricity generators.
"Final preparations for launch are on schedule," NASA test director Doug Lyons said. "We are not working any issues or concerns at this time."

Columbia's crew of five astronauts is due to spend 16 days in orbit conducting scientific research with a pair of free-flying satellites. Two spacewalks are also planned, to practice for the construction of the international space station.
